newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fischler calls for sharp increase in BSE research.
newsitem.headline: Fischler calls for sharp increase in BSE research.

text.p: Research into mad cow disease must be substantially and urgently increased, European Union Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Wednesday.
Priorities include establishing whether the disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) has been transmitted to humans, and developing tests for the disease in live animals and people.
A British government announcement in March that BSE could be passed to humans in the form of Creutzfeldt Jakob Disease triggered a a public health scare and collapse in consumer confidence in beef.

"There are still major gaps in our knowledge of the disease," Fischler said in a statement, adding that further research was needed both to protect human health and to eradicate the disease as quickly as possible.
The lack of scientific knowledge on BSE made it difficult to deal with the crisis in a rational and methodical way, he added.
Fischler was commenting after a group of independent scientists headed by Professor Charles Weissmann of Zurich University presented a report on BSE research priorities.

In addition to transmission of BSE to humans and live tests, Weissmann suggested an assessment of the disease risk from the use in human food products of brains and other suspect animal tissue before they were banned, the statement said.
Research was also required into whether other animal tissue could be a source of BSE infection, it said.

Further research was also needed into the way in which BSE was passed from cows to calves, whether the BSE agent was different from the scrapie agent in sheep and into the nature of the BSE infectious agent known as the "prion."
